title: "The Student-t distribution"
execute:

Standardizing a sample mean with an estimated standard deviation adds uncertainty. Under independent normal sampling, the resulting statistic follows a **Student-$t$ distribution**, which has heavier tails than the standard normal.

## Construction

If $Z\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$, $Q\sim\chi^2_\nu$, and $Z$ is independent of $Q$, then

$$
T=\frac{Z}{\sqrt{Q/\nu}}\sim t_\nu.
$$

For independent normal differences $D_1,\ldots,D_n$ with population mean $\mu_D$,

$$
\overline D=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nD_i,
\qquad
S_D^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(D_i-\overline D)^2,
$$

$$
T
=\frac{\overline D-\mu_D}{S_D/\sqrt n}
\sim t_{n-1}.
$$

The centered differences obey

$$
\sum_{i=1}^n(D_i-\overline D)=0,
$$

so only $n-1$ deviations vary freely. The density is symmetric,
$f_T(-t)=f_T(t)$, and for $c>0$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(|T|\geq c)=2\mathbb{P}(T\geq c).
$$

As $\nu$ increases, estimating the scale matters less and the $t$ density approaches the standard-normal density.

## Paired acoustic measurements

Hillenbrand et al. recorded each speaker producing both /ae/ in *had* and /i/ in *heed*. We preserve that pairing and define $D$ as F1(/ae/) minus F1(/i/) in hertz.

```{r}
#| label: hillenbrand-student-t
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv(
  "data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
ae <- subset(vowels, vowel == "{", select = c(speaker_id, speaker_type, f1_hz))
names(ae)[3] <- "f1_ae_hz"
i <- subset(vowels, vowel == "i", select = c(speaker_id, speaker_type, f1_hz))
names(i)[3] <- "f1_i_hz"
paired <- merge(ae, i, by = c("speaker_id", "speaker_type"))
paired$difference_hz <- paired$f1_ae_hz - paired$f1_i_hz

n <- nrow(paired)
mean_difference <- mean(paired$difference_hz)
sd_difference <- sd(paired$difference_hz)
standard_error <- sd_difference / sqrt(n)
t_observed <- mean_difference / standard_error
df <- n - 1L

t_grid <- data.frame(t = seq(-4, 4, length.out = 600L))
t_grid$t_density <- dt(t_grid$t, df = df)
t_grid$normal_density <- dnorm(t_grid$t)

stopifnot(
  n == 139L,
  !anyDuplicated(paired$speaker_id),
  all(is.finite(paired$difference_hz)),
  df == 138L
)

data.frame(n, mean_difference, sd_difference, standard_error,
           t_observed, df)
```

The observed mean difference is `r sprintf("%.1f", mean_difference)` Hz, with standard error `r sprintf("%.2f", standard_error)` Hz. Relative to a zero-difference reference, the standardized statistic is `r sprintf("%.2f", t_observed)` with `r df` degrees of freedom. This calculation describes the paired measurements; its sampling interpretation still requires the model assumptions above.

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-paired-differences
#| fig-cap: "Observed within-speaker F1 differences. The accent line marks the observed mean; the dashed line marks zero."
ggplot(paired, aes(difference_hz)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 18, fill = "grey75", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey25", linetype = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean_difference, color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Within-speaker F1 difference: /ae/ minus /i/ (Hz)",
       y = "Speakers") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-t-reference
#| fig-cap: "The t reference determined by the paired sample size, compared with a standard-normal density."
ggplot(t_grid, aes(t)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = normal_density), color = "grey45", linetype = 2,
            linewidth = 0.75) +
  geom_line(aes(y = t_density), color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.85) +
  labs(x = "Standardized statistic", y = "Reference density") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Check your understanding

1. Recompute the paired differences by reshaping rather than merging.
2. Why is the speaker, rather than the vowel token, the paired unit?
3. Compare `dt()` and `dnorm()` farther into the tails.
4. What assumption is needed to interpret the displayed $t$ density as the statistic's sampling distribution?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Reshaping to one row per speaker reproduces 139 /ae/–/i/ F1 differences with mean 250.964 Hz and standard deviation 81.665 Hz. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The speaker is the paired unit because each difference combines that speaker's /ae/ and /i/ tokens; the two vowel tokens are the measurements being paired. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Farther from zero, the $t_{138}$ density and tail probabilities exceed their standard-normal counterparts because estimating scale produces heavier tails. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The $t_{138}$ density is a sampling reference for the paired Hillenbrand F1 statistic only if the speaker-level differences are independent normal draws, or an approximation is justified. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
